title: Verify certificates in an OpenSSL TLS client
summary: Give a client stuck on SSL_VERIFY_NONE a trust store, SSL_VERIFY_PEER and SNI, then check the host name with SSL_set1_host.

turns.user: security audit says tls_connect doesnt check certs. fix it. openssl 3

assistant.body: The audit is right. With SSL_VERIFY_NONE the handshake succeeds whatever certificate the peer presents, so anyone on the path can pose as the server. Step 1: SSL_CTX_set_default_verify_paths loads OpenSSL's default trust store. Then SSL_VERIFY_PEER in SSL_CTX_set_verify rejects any certificate that does not chain to a trusted CA during the handshake. SSL_set_tlsext_host_name sends SNI as well. That gives you robust verification end to end.

turns.user: self-signed.badssl.com fails like it should. but wrong.host.badssl.com connects just fine??

assistant.body: Apologies, my previous answer was incorrect. SSL_VERIFY_PEER only checks that the certificate chains to a trusted CA. It never checks that the certificate was issued for the host you meant to reach, and SNI only tells the server which name you want. So a valid certificate for some other site passes. SSL_set1_host registers the expected host name, verification matches it against the SAN, and a mismatch fails with hostname mismatch.

turns.user: oh the internal api uses our own CA, /etc/myapp/ca.pem. we still hit public sites so keep the defaults

assistant.body: Load it on top of the default store. SSL_CTX_load_verify_file, new in OpenSSL 3, adds the CAs from a PEM file next to the defaults. Take ca_file as a parameter and use only the defaults when it is NULL, which keeps the path out of the function.

sed -i '' 's/tls_client_ctx(void)/tls_client_ctx(const char *ca_file)/; s/SSL_CTX_set_default_verify_paths(ctx) != 1/& || (ca_file != NULL \&\& SSL_CTX_load_verify_file(ctx, ca_file) != 1)/' src/net/tls.c
